newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak May inflation lower, but seen accelerating.
newsitem.headline: Slovak May inflation lower, but seen accelerating.

text.p: Slovak consumer inflation (CPI) continued its favourable downtrend in May, but analysts warned that high interest rates and expansive budget spending could lead to its acceleration later in the year.
The Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) on Tuesday released May CPI data showing a 0.1 percent month-on-month increase, putting annual inflation at 6.1 percent.
The 1997 state budget is based on an assumed annual inflation rate of up to six percent.
"The latest CPI figure is surprisingly good, but I doubt that the favourable trend can be maintained over a longer term," said an analyst of a foreign bank.

Analysts said that after months of lowering, CPI is poised to accelerate mainly due to high rates on the local money market and expected budgetary expenditures for projects which have yet to come from state coffers.

"There is a huge disproportion between interbank rates ranging from 30 to 40 percent and the inflation rate at some six percent...these two factors will have to approach each other," said the analyst, who did not wish to be named.
Slovak interbank rates have been hovering above 30 percent for several weeks due to an acute shortage of market liquidity resulting from the central bank's fight to maintain currency stability.

Slovak companies often draw short-term crown loans to refinance their activities and analysts warn that the high cost of credits can push producer prices up and also spark consumer inflation pressure.
Analysts said one way to prevent a radical increase in inflation could be to revise government spending plans, especially on infrastructure projects.
The 1997 budget forecasts a 36.9 billion crown deficit (after a 25.5 billion crown shortfall in 1996) and allocates about 14 billion crowns for motorway construction.

Martin Barto of ING Barings saw modest inflationary pressure in the near term and predicted an annual rate at around 6.5 percent during the next three months. But he also warned of a possible CPI acceleration in the autumn.

"We do not expect a dramatic increase in inflation in coming months as the crown still has not depreciated, the budget deficit trend is so far favourable and the government is still not planning deregulation of state-controlled energy prices and rents," Barto said.

"(But) we also cannot predict crown movements until September -- the currency appears likely to weaken -- and we still do not know whether the government will carry out more expansive programmes in the autumn which could negatively influence the inflation rate," he added.
The state budget recorded a deficit of 4.692 billion crowns for the first four months of this year, up from 3.45 billion for the first quarter.
